Integrating ecological knowledge across planning, forestry, education, and environmental agencies is essential if urban forests are to realize their full climate adaptation potential (Pauleit et al., 2017;Singh et al., 2024). Finally, equitable access to trees and green infrastructure must become a central objective of urban planning, particularly in rapidly urbanizing regions where vulnerable communities face disproportionate exposure to climaterelated risks (United Nations, 2024;WHO, 2021). Despite these advances, important knowledge gaps remain. Greater attention is needed to long-term monitoring under compound climate extremes, economic valuation of ecosystem services, innovative financing mechanisms, governance effectiveness, and the integration of ecological science with urban des

title: Economic Policy Uncertainty in the 2020s: Measurement, Conditional Effects, and a Future Research Agenda
source: International Journal of Academic Research in Accounting Finance and Management Sciences
summary: HRMARS - Economic policy uncertainty (EPU) has developed from a macro-level news index into a multilevel construct explaining heterogeneous corporate decisions, information environments, and market outcomes. This article critically integrat
content: HRMARS - Economic policy uncertainty (EPU) has developed from a macro-level news index into a multilevel construct explaining heterogeneous corporate decisions, information environments, and market outcomes. This article critically integrates thirty-one peer-reviewed studies from 2020 to 2025, alongside four foundational contributions that delimit the construct and its core mechanisms. The review organizes contemporary evidence around three questions: how EPU is measured, through which mechanisms it affects firms, and why its consequences vary across settings. National news-based indices remain influential but are increasingly complemented by local, policy-specific, survey-based, and firm-level textual measures. Across investment, financing, innovation, and disclosure, the dominant pattern is conditional: real-options delay and financing frictions produce contraction, while precautionary liquidity, accelerated innovation, and timely disclosure reflect adaptive responses under specific governance and institutional conditions. An integrated framework is advanced in which measured uncertainty operates through managerial perception and is moderated by firm resources, industry irreversibility, and political-institutional context. A research agenda is proposed for firm-level and LLM-enabled measurement, multilevel causal designs, and strategic resilience, with particular attention to financial statement comparability as a mechanism linking policy uncertainty, strategic differentiation, and reporting credibility.

title: The Effects of Sustainable Development Goals, Digital Currency, Board Independence, And Macroeconomic Factors on Banking Performance in Indonesia: The Mediating Role of Third-Party Funds
source: Journal of Economics Finance and Management Studies
summary: This study aims to examine the effect of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), Digital Currency, Board Independence and macroeconomic factors proxied by Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and Inflation on banking performance in Indonesia. It also
content: This study aims to examine the effect of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), Digital Currency, Board Independence and macroeconomic factors proxied by Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and Inflation on banking performance in Indonesia. It also investigates the mediating role of Third-Party Funds (Customer Deposits) in the relationship between these independent variables and banking performance. This research employs a quantitative approach using panel data regression analysis. The sample consists of 34 banking companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during the observation period 2015 - 2024. The empirical results reveal that GDP has a positive and significant effect on banking performance, while Inflation has a negative and significant effect on ROA. Board Independence also significantly affects banking performance. SDGs and Digital Currency demonstrate direct effects on performance; however, Third-Party Funds do not mediate the relationship between SDGs, Digital Currency, Board Independence, GDP, and Inflation and banking performance. Theoretically, this study extends Financial Intermediation Theory by demonstrating that deposit mobilization does not necessarily serve as the primary transmission channel in improving banking performance. From managerial and policy perspectives, the findings emphasize the importance of strengthening asset quality, risk management, operational efficiency, and macroeconomic stability in sustaining banking performance amid digital transformation and sustainability demands. However, this study is limited by the use of proxy variables to measure SDGs and Digital Currency, which may not fully capture the multidimensional nature of these concepts, the relatively limited observation period that may not reflect long-term structural effects, and the use of Third-Party Funds as the sole mediating variable. Future research is recommended to consider alternative mediating variables and extend the observation period to obtain more comprehensive findings.

title: Do ESG Perceptions Discipline Irrational Investing Among Generation Z Investors?
summary: This study aims to examine the effects of herding behavior, overconfidence bias, and loss aversion bias on the investment decisions of Generation Z investors in Indonesia and to investigate the moderating role of Environmental, Social, and
content: This study aims to examine the effects of herding behavior, overconfidence bias, and loss aversion bias on the investment decisions of Generation Z investors in Indonesia and to investigate the moderating role of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) perception. A quantitative approach with an associative-causal survey design was employed. Data were collected from Indonesian Generation Z investors using purposive sampling and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that herding behavior and overconfidence bias positively influence investment decisions, whereas loss aversion bias has no significant effect. ESG perception moderates the effects of overconfidence bias and loss aversion bias but does not moderate the effect of herding behavior. These findings suggest that ESG perception selectively moderates behavioral biases, with implications for ESG literacy and investment decision-making among Generation Z investors

title: China in Myanmar
summary: This book explores the complex power dynamics shaping China-Myanmar relations within the framework of asymmetrical geopolitics. By examining disparities in resources, influence and capacity, it delves into how China leverages its economic a
content: This book explores the complex power dynamics shaping China-Myanmar relations within the framework of asymmetrical geopolitics. By examining disparities in resources, influence and capacity, it delves into how China leverages its economic and strategic dominance, particularly through the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). It provides a nuanced understanding of Myanmar’s geopolitical significance as a site of competition and its delicate balance between dependence on China and autonomy. The book highlights China’s asymmetric foreign policy strategies, the impact of the 2021 Military Coup on bilateral relations, and the challenges posed by stalled BRI projects amidst ethnic conflict and local resistance. It also examines the socio-political and economic implications of China’s investments in Myanmar, addressing issues pertaining to migration, ethnic ties and security. Through rigorous analysis, the book connects these elements to broader South Asian geopolitics, emphasizing Myanmar’s pivotal role in China’s regional ambitions and its access to the Indian Ocean. This interdisciplinary volume is an essential resource for scholars, researchers and students in International Relations, South Asian studies, Area Studies, Global Studies and Geopolitics. Additionally, journalists, policymakers and academics interested in China’s rise, the Belt and Road Initiative and South Asian geopolitics will find this book insightful.

title: Engineering the Intelligent Enterprise: The Complete Guide to Data and AI Platform Engineering
summary: The company is in a new digital transformation era. The evolution of the organizations has progressed from transaction processing and enterprise integration to business intelligence, cloud computing, big data, machine learning, gen AI and n
content: The company is in a new digital transformation era. The evolution of the organizations has progressed from transaction processing and enterprise integration to business intelligence, cloud computing, big data, machine learning, gen AI and now towards autonomous and agentic systems. However, technology is not intelligence, in an organization. This is no longer solely a matter of gathering more data, implementing more models and using the newest artificial intelligence tools. That's the challenge of how to create an enterprise-level capability that can help continuously convert observations into trusted information, information into insights and prediction, and knowledge into intelligence, and intelligence into governed actions leading to measurable results. This book tackles this issue from the engineering, architectural, operational and governance standpoint. The case for enterprise intelligence is defined as the socio-technical capability connecting a system of data, platforms, analytics, machine learning, generative AI, knowledge systems, autonomous agents, humans, processes, policies and feedback mechanisms. It is a technology-agnostic view that elevates decision quality, operational reliability and assured autonomy, learning, and business value to the heart of enterprise transformation. The book consists of a collection of Enterprise Intelligence Lifecycle, linking together data, information, insights, predictions, knowledge, intelligence, actions, and governed autonomy, all in an iterative process of continuous feedback. It's important to note that the lifecycle is not being presented as a straight technology pipeline. Each step raises semantic, ownership, reliability, security, governance, accountability and measurable value issues. The right idea is that intelligence is only an enterprise capability when technical products are linked to actual decisions, processes, stewards, process controls and outcomes. As such, the manuscript views intelligence as a continuously evolving product that is engineered to be an enterprise endeavor, and not anything specific like an isolated dashboard, machine learning model, chatbot, or AI agent. Chapter 1 lays the foundation for the concepts and architecture of the intelligent enterprise. It helps you define and distinguish between a data-driven organization and an intelligence-driven organization, while also introducing the Enterprise Intelligence Lifecycle, layered reference architecture, capability domains, maturity model, value measurement framework, principles of governance and an implementation blueprint. One key theme is keeping the goal based on appropriate and governed autonomy rather than the goal in front of it being maximum autonomy and automation. There must be a balance of autonomy to consequence, uncertainty, reversibility, level of evidence, permissions and escalation requirements. The second chapter focuses on Intelligence on the Platform. title: From Tenure Security to Inequality Reproduction: Reassessing Indonesia's PTSL Program Through a Structural Poverty Lens
summary: This article investigates the effectiveness of the Complete Systematic Land Registration (PTSL) program in addressing structural poverty in rural Indonesia, using Parungsari Village in Lebak Regency, Banten Province, as a case study. Althou
content: This article investigates the effectiveness of the Complete Systematic Land Registration (PTSL) program in addressing structural poverty in rural Indonesia, using Parungsari Village in Lebak Regency, Banten Province, as a case study. Although PTSL was introduced to improve tenure security, legal certainty, and access to capital, its implementation reveals tensions between legalizing land ownership and enduring agrarian inequalities. The study applies a mixed-methods case study approach, showing that community participation is the most influential factor shaping the program’s outcomes, followed by land productivity, the use of agricultural technology, certificate ownership, and access to agricultural credit. Empirical results indicate that the program disproportionately advantages large and absentee landowners, while smallholders and landless groups receive limited benefit. Instead of reducing inequality, land certification often reinforces existing class-based divisions and demonstrates limited measurable impact on household welfare or agricultural productivity. The article argues that PTSL can contribute to poverty reduction only when integrated into a broader agrarian reform framework that couples asset legalization with improved access to agrarian resources. Policy implications highlight the need to prevent and resolve agrarian conflicts, strengthen community capacity and post-certification support, and implement an integrated agrarian reform strategy to promote equitable rural development and address structural poverty.

title: Integrating risk and feasibility in the spatial planning of nature-based solutions: a cross-city analysis of Barcelona, Boston, and Rotterdam
summary: Abstract Urban areas increasingly turn to nature-based solutions (NbS) to adapt to climate-related risks, which require integrated and systemic planning evaluating risks and feasibility of implementation. Here we develop a transferable, SET
content: Abstract Urban areas increasingly turn to nature-based solutions (NbS) to adapt to climate-related risks, which require integrated and systemic planning evaluating risks and feasibility of implementation. Here we develop a transferable, SETS-based decision-support framework that spatially analyzes multi-hazard climate risk and feasibility for four NbS types: green roofs, permeable pavements, rain gardens, and urban parks, across Barcelona, Boston, and Rotterdam. Integrating spatial and statistical analyses, we identify where different kinds of NbS are both most needed and most feasible for mitigating urban flooding and heat stress. Results reveal strong spatial clustering of risks and feasibility across all cities, with heat risk showing the highest spatial autocorrelation. Across cases, green roofs and permeable pavements consistently exhibit high feasibility in dense, heat-prone urban areas, whereas rain gardens and urban parks are constrained by land availability and underground infrastructure. The comparative analysis highlights how urban morphology, governance structures, and socio-economic factors shape feasibility for NbS implementation. Overlaying risk and feasibility identifies priority high risk –high feasibility zones for rapid implementation and flags high-risk/low-feasibility neighborhoods where infrastructure deficits and vulnerability may constrain adaptation, supporting more justice-oriented, context-sensitive NbS planning.

title: ESG Blockholders and Corporate Green Bonds
summary: Abstract This study explores whether ESG blockholders (large shareholders with a focus on environmental, social, and governance issues) influence the issuance of corporate green bonds, which fund environmentally friendly projects. The findi
content: Abstract This study explores whether ESG blockholders (large shareholders with a focus on environmental, social, and governance issues) influence the issuance of corporate green bonds, which fund environmentally friendly projects. The findings show that ESG blockholders positively impact green bond issuance, benefiting shareholders by reducing external financing costs in the long term. Additionally, ESG blockholders modify the relationship between green bond issuance and debt financing costs, helping mitigate the limited long-term effects of green bonds on borrowing costs. After climate policy shocks, ESG blockholders emphasize green actions, driving more green bond issuances to manage environmental risks. This highlights the role of large investors in promoting green bond markets.

title: Microfinance as a Catalyst for Women’s Empowerment: Evidence from Uttarakhand
summary: Microfinance offers numerous benefits to women, particularly those residing in financially constrained areas. This study investigates the effects of microfinance on women in Uttarakhand, aiming to determine whether it helps them generate in
content: Microfinance offers numerous benefits to women, particularly those residing in financially constrained areas. This study investigates the effects of microfinance on women in Uttarakhand, aiming to determine whether it helps them generate income and gain greater autonomy.We collected data using various techniques, including surveys and interviews. The findings indicate that microfinance assists women in certain areas, such as earning income and boosting their self-esteem. However, it does not consistently enhance decision-making power at home or social mobility.The study reveals that microfinance alone is insufficient to empower women.They also require education and institutional backing, along with policies that address the specific challenges faced by female workers.Although microfinance can be a useful tool, it is merely one component of a broader solution. This research sheds light on the role of microfinance in promoting equal opportunities, especially in economically weaker regions like Uttarakhand.

title: Extended hydrothermal aging and glass infiltration on minimally processed recycled 3Y-TZP: microstructural and optical properties
summary: This study evaluated the effects of glass infiltration and hydrothermal aging on the microstructural and optical properties of minimally processed recycled 3Y-TZP. Unprocessed 3Y-TZP remnants were milled into powder, compacted into discs, a
content: This study evaluated the effects of glass infiltration and hydrothermal aging on the microstructural and optical properties of minimally processed recycled 3Y-TZP. Unprocessed 3Y-TZP remnants were milled into powder, compacted into discs, and sintered. Specimens were divided into six groups according to glass infiltration and hydrothermal aging (immediate, 50 h, and 100 h at 134 °C/2.2 bar). Particle size was measured by laser diffraction. Density and optical properties (contrast ratio and translucency) were longitudinally evaluated on the same specimens using Archimedes' principle and reflectance measurements (n = 10), whereas crystalline phases (Raman spectroscopy, n = 3), surface and cross-sectional morphology (n = 3), and elemental composition (n = 3) were analyzed on independent specimens allocated to each experimental condition. Color stability and translucency variation were compared with perceptibility (PT = 0.81; TPT = 0.62) and acceptability (AT = 1.77; TAT = 2.62) thresholds (n = 10). Density data were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures ANOVA, while optical properties were analyzed using two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, followed by Tukey's post hoc test. Mean particle size of recycled powder was 1.61 μm. Relative densities for immediate, 50 h, and 100 h groups were 99.68%, 99.24%, and 99.04%. Raman spectra revealed predominance of tetragonal-cubic phases in immediate non-infiltrated group, while monoclinic phase prevailed in others. SEM showed homogeneous surfaces. EDS confirmed zirconium, yttrium, and hafnium in non-infiltrated groups, and silicon, aluminum, sodium, potassium, and calcium in infiltrated. Non-infiltrated groups showed lower contrast ratio and greater translucency than infiltrated, independent of aging. Aging minimally affected optical properties, except infiltrated specimens, where translucency was higher immediately than after 50-100 h. All groups exhibited color and translucency variation below perceptibility and acceptability thresholds. Prolonged hydrothermal degradation influenced the microstructural and optical features of recycled 3Y-TZP, while glass infiltration further modified these characteristics, reducing translucency while increasing opacity and color stability.

title: 3D-printing for zirconia abutment manufacturing and screw access hole effect: fatigue behavior of milled zirconia simplified restorations
summary: The aim of this study is to evaluate the effect of the abutment manufacturing method (CAD/CAM milling or 3D-printing) and the presence of a screw access hole on the fatigue behavior of adhesively cemented zirconia restorations. Zirconia (3Y
content: The aim of this study is to evaluate the effect of the abutment manufacturing method (CAD/CAM milling or 3D-printing) and the presence of a screw access hole on the fatigue behavior of adhesively cemented zirconia restorations. Zirconia (3YSZ) discs, representing prosthetic abutments (Ø= 10 mm, 3 mm in thickness) were fabricated by simulated CAD/CAM milling (M) or lithography-based 3D-printing (3D), either with a screw access hole (Ø=2.5 mm, filled with resin composite) or without (Rigid) and allocated into four groups: M-Screw, M-Rigid, 3D-Screw and 3D-Rigid. Restorative zirconia discs (4YSZ; Ø=10 mm, 1 mm thickness) were adhesively cemented to the abutments using a dual-cure resin cemented. Cyclic fatigue test was performed (n = 15). Data were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier, Log-rank (Mantel-Cox) and Two-way ANOVA supplemented by fractography and finite element analysis. No significant effect of the manufacturing method was observed on fatigue behavior (p ≥ 0.05). Rigid groups exhibited no failures during testing. Conversely, the presence of a screw access hole significantly reduced fatigue behavior (p < 0.05), with similar mean fatigue failure loads for 3D-Screw (2,286 N) and M-Screw (2,273 N) groups. The manufacturing method of the zirconia abutments (3D-printing or milling) did not influence the fatigue behavior of the restorations. However, the presence of a screw access hole in the abutments significantly reduced the fatigue behavior of the specimen.

title: The research landscape of bureaucracy and sustainable development: A bibliometric analysis
summary: Bureaucracy plays an important role in translating sustainable development goals into policies and administrative practices, yet its contribution to sustainability remains fragmented in the academic literature. This study aims to examine th
content: Bureaucracy plays an important role in translating sustainable development goals into policies and administrative practices, yet its contribution to sustainability remains fragmented in the academic literature. This study aims to examine the development, thematic evolution, and collaboration patterns of research on bureaucracy and sustainable development. A bibliometric analysis was conducted using publications indexed in Scopus and analyzed with the Bibliometrix package in R. The analysis examined publication trends, authors, institutions, countries, keywords, thematic structures, and collaboration networks. The findings show a steady increase in scholarly publications, particularly following the adoption of the United Nations 2030 Agenda and the Paris Agreement. Bureaucracy emerges as a conceptually central but relatively underdeveloped theme compared with environmental policy, environmental protection, and climate change. Keyword trends also indicate a shift from governance and policy integration toward bureaucratic reform, digital transformation, innovation, and adaptive governance. Collaboration networks remain fragmented, while international research is largely concentrated in advanced economies, with developing countries playing a more limited role. These findings indicate that bureaucracy can function both as an enabler and a barrier to sustainable development depending on institutional capacity and governance context. The study highlights the need for stronger theoretical integration, context-sensitive research, and more inclusive international collaboration to strengthen the role of bureaucracy in advancing sustainable development.

title: A Scopus-based scientometric and conceptual mapping study of Artificial Intelligence and machine learning in ESG and sustainable finance
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) integrated with a broader environmental, social, and governance (ESG) framework are a cutting-edge topic in the realm of sustainable finance academic research. This study conducts a com
content: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) integrated with a broader environmental, social, and governance (ESG) framework are a cutting-edge topic in the realm of sustainable finance academic research. This study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric and science mapping analysis of 1,083 journal articles and reviews published between 2001 and 2025. The three primary research objectives guiding our investigation included: (1) Who are the most highly influential contributors to this area? (2) What are the growing collaborations within the academic publishing community? and (3) What are the most prominent academic research themes emerging at this point? The Analysis is done using Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny packages using R and VOSviewer software. We employed performance analysis, co-authorship network analysis, bibliographic coupling, keyword co-occurrence mapping, thematic analysis, and Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA). This bibliometric analysis illustrates that from 2019 onward, there has been an exponential increase in research publications, reaching a total of 442 published articles in the year 2025. Science mapping identifies distinct research clusters, including AI applications in ESG performance measurement, digital transformation, green finance, and climate analysis. However, the themes relating to CSR and Governance are less deeply or uniformly integrated into the growth of AI/ML research and therefore remain theoretical constructs existing in an isolated state without a broad general applicability across multiple areas of finance technology development. The findings of this study provide evidence of the rapid advancement of this area of sustainable finance research.

title: Labor force shifts in the Midwest during the pandemic: role of human capital and geography
summary: Abstract The labor force participation rate (LFPR) in Midwestern counties declined from 2019 to 2021, following national trends but less sharply. Early in the pandemic, declines in LFPR were associated with reduced participation among older
content: Abstract The labor force participation rate (LFPR) in Midwestern counties declined from 2019 to 2021, following national trends but less sharply. Early in the pandemic, declines in LFPR were associated with reduced participation among older workers, in metro areas, and in counties highly vulnerable to the pandemic, while higher participation among Whites, female, and educated workers was associated with partially offsetting these losses. Metro areas with higher LFPR among individuals with children under age 6 and greater in-migration experienced smaller initial declines. By 2020–2021, patterns shifted: younger workers, manufacturing-dependent employment, and human capital were linked to sharper drops. Meanwhile, mid-career workers, educated labor, individuals with young children, and in-migration in metro areas helped moderate declines, highlighting complex regional and demographic dynamics.

title: Bridging Urban AI and Responsible AI Toward Collective Urban Intelligence: Insights From 14 African Initiatives
summary: Urban artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a transformative paradigm redefining how cities process data, make decisions, and address systemic challenges. Yet, in African contexts, AI adoption remains constrained by infrastructural li
content: Urban artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a transformative paradigm redefining how cities process data, make decisions, and address systemic challenges. Yet, in African contexts, AI adoption remains constrained by infrastructural limitations, governance gaps, unequal access to technology, and lack of context‐sensitive approaches. This article explores the intersection of urban AI, responsible AI, and collective urban intelligence (CUI) to understand how African initiatives are leveraging AI to foster sustainable, inclusive, and ethical urban transformation processes. Drawing on 14 semi‐structured interviews with practitioners, researchers, and entrepreneurs from across the continent, the study maps the current landscape of AI‐driven tools and services addressing sectors such as planning, health, agriculture, and education. The findings reveal that African‐led AI initiatives are operationalizing key responsible AI principles, showcasing how CUI is promoting distributed intelligence systems where human, institutional, and algorithmic agents co‐produce locally relevant urban knowledge.

title: Rethinking Sustainable Development Through the Lens of Public Finance
summary: This chapter examines sustainable development through the lens of public finance, arguing that fiscal systems are critical for advancing economic, social, and environmental sustainability. Achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
content: This chapter examines sustainable development through the lens of public finance, arguing that fiscal systems are critical for advancing economic, social, and environmental sustainability. Achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) requires substantial financial resources and responsive governance. The study explores how public finance drives sustainability through domestic resource mobilisation, strategic fiscal policies, and targeted expenditure. However, financing sustainability is constrained by a US$4 trillion global financing gap, rising public debt, institutional weaknesses, and climate risks. To overcome these barriers, the chapter highlights emerging trends like Green Public Financial Management (Green PFM), ESG integration, and sustainable bonds. It proposes a Public Finance Framework for Sustainable Development linking financial inputs and governance processes to long-term impacts. The chapter concludes that integrating sustainability into fiscal planning is a fundamental necessity for resilient, inclusive well-being.

title: Changing inflation perception and the propagation of news shocks
summary: Abstract Based on a previously established text data-based indicator, the Inflation Perception Indicator (IPI), we analyze the information content of inflation-related media coverage. It is argued that media do not report on inflation in a
content: Abstract Based on a previously established text data-based indicator, the Inflation Perception Indicator (IPI), we analyze the information content of inflation-related media coverage. It is argued that media do not report on inflation in a constant or systematic manner but instead react to specific events, which means that reporting is state-dependent. Using a dynamic extension of the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling approach we examine the salience and framing of inflation in a corpus of 50,000 articles published by major German newspapers between 2001 and 2024. This approach allows to decompose the IPI into dynamic topic-specific subindicators. To analyze the information content of these newly constructed indicators, we estimate a threshold Bayesian Vector AutoRegressive (BVAR) model for variables from a New Keynesian macroeconomic model with two inflation regimes. Our results suggest that the topic-specific IPI subindicators contain different information about price developments. Moreover, we find some evidence that households make different use of this information in high- and low-inflation regimes when adjusting their inflation expectations.

title: Leadership for India’s Development: A Theoretical and Conceptual Understanding
source: Advanced International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research
summary: This research examines leadership as a decisive factor in India’s transition to a developed nation. It develops a historical, theoretical, and conceptual framework focusing on ethical legitimacy, strong institutions, strategic vision, state
content: This research examines leadership as a decisive factor in India’s transition to a developed nation. It develops a historical, theoretical, and conceptual framework focusing on ethical legitimacy, strong institutions, strategic vision, state capacity, inclusive governance, reform discipline, knowledge-based modernisation, and responsible geopolitical leadership.

title: Inflation, Geo-Economic Fragmentation, and Transforming Green Public Financial Administration
summary: The contemporary global economy is shaped by geo-economic fragmentation, geopolitical conflict, and systemic shocks, intensifying inflationary pressures across advanced and emerging economies and altering conditions for public financial adm
content: The contemporary global economy is shaped by geo-economic fragmentation, geopolitical conflict, and systemic shocks, intensifying inflationary pressures across advanced and emerging economies and altering conditions for public financial administration. Inflation has become a chronic structural feature that constrains fiscal capacity, reshapes distributive outcomes, and challenges long-term public investment. This chapter argues that inflation is a governance challenge embedded in public financial administration, not merely a monetary phenomenon. Drawing on macroeconomics, welfare economics, and public finance, it examines how inflation interacts with fiscal governance, social equity, and sustainability-oriented public finance under geo-economic instability. Using Green Public Financial Management (GPFM), it proposes an approach aligning macroeconomic stabilization, distributive justice, and climate-resilient development, emphasizing adaptive fiscal governance, progressive policies, and institutional innovation to reconcile inflation control with green investment and inclusive growth.

title: Determinants of Employee Performance in The Automotive Retail Sector: The Roles of Workload, Work Discipline, and Organizational Culture
summary: Good performance is a step toward achieving organizational goals; therefore, performance is also a key determinant in achieving these goals, making it necessary to strive to improve employee performance. One factor that influences employee
content: Good performance is a step toward achieving organizational goals; therefore, performance is also a key determinant in achieving these goals, making it necessary to strive to improve employee performance. One factor that influences employee performance is workload. By assigning an effective workload, employers can assess how much an employee can handle and the impact on their performance. In addition to workload, another factor that can influence employee performance is work discipline. Work discipline also serves to enhance individuals’ awareness and willingness to comply with all company regulations and prevailing social norms. In addition to workload and work discipline, another factor that can influence employee performance is organizational culture. The objective of this study is to examine and analyze the influence of workload, work discipline, and organizational culture on employee performance. This study was conducted at CV. Yamaha Waja Motor Hayam Wuruk Denpasar. The population for this study consists of all employees at CV. Yamaha Waja Motor’s Hayam Wuruk Branch in Denpasar, totaling 35 individuals. The sample size for this study was determined using a census method. The data analysis technique employed was multiple linear regression analysis. The results indicate that workload has a negative and significant effect on employee performance, work discipline has a positive and significant effect on employee performance, and organizational culture has a positive and significant effect on employee performance.

title: The Integration of Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Community Engagement in Sustainable Public Finance Administration
summary: This chapter examines the limitations of South Africa's public financial administration (PFA) in responding to climate change, environmental risk, and inequality. Drawing on recent flooding events, it argues that current financial governanc
content: This chapter examines the limitations of South Africa's public financial administration (PFA) in responding to climate change, environmental risk, and inequality. Drawing on recent flooding events, it argues that current financial governance remains largely reactive, technocratic, and insufficiently responsive to localised vulnerabilities, with those most affected often having limited influence over decision-making. While green finance initiatives signal progress, they frequently privilege formal expertise over locally grounded knowledge systems. The chapter contends that sustainable public financial governance requires the integration of indigenous knowledge systems (IKS) and meaningful community participation. Grounded in Ubuntu, it reframes governance as relational and participatory, proposing a framework centred on epistemic pluralism, participatory budgeting, and resilience-oriented expenditure to enhance effectiveness, legitimacy, and long-term sustainability.

title: A Study on the Role of Government Schemes and Policies in Collaboration with NABARD
summary: Rural development in India is pursued through an extensive architecture of government schemes and policies that are increasingly implemented in partnership with the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD). As the apex d
content: Rural development in India is pursued through an extensive architecture of government schemes and policies that are increasingly implemented in partnership with the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD). As the apex development bank for agriculture and rural areas, NABARD functions as a bridge between policy formulation and grassroots implementation by providing refinance, developmental support, capacity building and policy feedback to government. This paper examines how government schemes and policies operate in collaboration with NABARD, focusing on credit linked interventions, infrastructure development, financial inclusion and climate resilient rural development. Drawing on secondary literature and recent assessments of NABARD’s operations, the paper analyses key collaborative mechanisms such as the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), government sponsored agricultural credit schemes, self help group (SHG) and joint liability models, and NABARD’s role as National Implementing Entity (NIE) for climate funds. The study finds that government–NABARD collaboration has significantly expanded rural credit, improved infrastructure and strengthened financial inclusion, but also reveals persisting gaps in awareness, coverage and sustainability of benefits. The paper concludes with policy recommendations to deepen integration between schemes, enhance outreach and leverage digital and climate finance innovations for inclusive rural growth.

title: The Evolution of Public Financial Administration in South Africa
summary: This chapter examines the evolution of South Africa's public financial administration (PFA) from apartheid to a democratic state. Using qualitative document analysis of post-1994 legislation and audit reports, it highlights the transition t
content: This chapter examines the evolution of South Africa's public financial administration (PFA) from apartheid to a democratic state. Using qualitative document analysis of post-1994 legislation and audit reports, it highlights the transition toward transparency, accountability, and equity. The study explores major legislative milestones like the 1996 Constitution, the Public Finance Management Act (PFMA), and the Municipal Finance Management Act (MFMA), which modernised governance. It outlines institutional transformations within the National Treasury, Auditor-General, and Revenue Service. Despite these reforms, systemic challenges persist, including corruption, weak municipal management, and capacity constraints. Finally, the study addresses emerging trends reshaping PFA, emphasizing the integration of Green Public Financial Management (Green PFM) for sustainable development and the role of digital transformation in improving efficiency and service delivery.

title: The role of internet banking and digital payment on financial inclusion: socioeconomic status as a moderator
source: Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting
summary: Abstract Financial inclusion (FI) is an important tool in creating economic growth and reducing poverty for social equity regardless of country’s development. This study examines the effects of Mobile and Internet Banking (MIB) and Digital
content: Abstract Financial inclusion (FI) is an important tool in creating economic growth and reducing poverty for social equity regardless of country’s development. This study examines the effects of Mobile and Internet Banking (MIB) and Digital Payment Systems (DPS) on financial inclusion in diverse economic environments. Additionally, it examines whether the SES plays any roles as a moderator on the relationships between digital financial services and financial inclusion. Using a panel of 63 countries in a cross-sectional database which is divided according to overall country grouping, state of development, income level and Human Development Index (HDI), four separate samples are analysed utilizing multiple regression and Feasible Generalized Least Squares (FGLS) technique. The findings of research are all consistently profound and positive in the impact of DPS on FI irrespective of country category or model, reemphasizing its wide applicability to financial inclusion. On the other hand, the impact of MIB is less effective or even counterproductive, particularly in countries with high income and HDI countries where there is a small share of conventional banking services exist. In certain models, SES has a moderating effect indicating a context sensitive relationship from SES to the role of digital tools on financial access.

title: The China factor in diaspora economic diplomacy: comparing Chinese and Indian transnational networks in Southeast Asia
summary: China and India are gradually using the overseas Chinese community to form economic ties, spread culture and knowledge, provide investment support, and offer diplomatic support. Diaspora engagement generally refers to a tool for soft power
content: China and India are gradually using the overseas Chinese community to form economic ties, spread culture and knowledge, provide investment support, and offer diplomatic support. Diaspora engagement generally refers to a tool for soft power projection or a bilateral relationship established between the government in the homeland and the expatriate community. Both ways in this paper fail to recognize the independence of diasporic communities and the political power of host countries. Singapore and Malaysia are selected as cases to compare China's increasingly coordinated party-state approach to overseas Chinese affairs with India's network-centred architecture of diaspora engagement. Building on Rajesh Rai's scholarship of transnational networks, changing identities and the demand to address migrants' new allegiances sensitively, this paper presents a host-state-embedded network system for diaspora economic diplomacy. It is thought that the impact of diaspora engagement depends on four interrelated conditions: the strength of connectivity with the homeland-state, the richness of transnational economic and social networks, the autonomy and host-country embedding of diaspora actors, and the ability to convert relationships into mutual economic benefits. China has institutional concentration that can rapidly mobilize resources and link business, talents and cultural networks, but it is also politically sensitive when ethnic ties are believed to have blurred the line between cultural ties and foreign political organisation. India has a less centralised system, and programmes such as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, Overseas Citizenship of India, knowledge networks and cultural engagement operate through relatively plural and voluntary associations. Singapore and Malaysia show that neither the Chinese nor the Indian communities can be considered extensions of the ancestral homeland. Citizenship, class, language, generation and the political system at home all shape people's identity and interests. Therefore, diaspora-based competition in Southeast Asia will not be a simple zero-sum game, according to the article. The more sustainable model is one in which diasporic networks act as bridges for trade, technology, entrepreneurship and social exchange, and host-state sovereignty and diaspora autonomy remain explicit constraints on engagement with the homeland.

title: Fabrication of sisal fiber-derived beads from sustainable solvents: investigating their potential for pH-responsive sorption of bovine serum albumin
summary: Abstract Gel beads were prepared from sisal fibers (SFs) by dissolving the treated biomass in green solvent systems (NaOH–urea and ZnCl 2 aqueous solutions), followed by regeneration in different coagulation media (HNO 3 , CaCl 2 , and etha
content: Abstract Gel beads were prepared from sisal fibers (SFs) by dissolving the treated biomass in green solvent systems (NaOH–urea and ZnCl 2 aqueous solutions), followed by regeneration in different coagulation media (HNO 3 , CaCl 2 , and ethanol). This sustainable strategy converts renewable sisal biomass into functional bio-based materials that serve as promising alternatives to fossil-derived polymers. The effects of dissolution and regeneration conditions on the physicochemical and structural properties of the resulting gel beads were systematically investigated. Distinct morphological, porosity, and swelling behaviors were observed depending on the processing method. Beads prepared using the NaOH–urea system showed compact, uniform pore structures with less swelling at higher SF content, whereas ZnCl 2 -activated beads displayed adjustable porosity and swelling influenced by the regeneration medium. Ethanol-coagulated beads exhibited an open pore network with the highest porosity (57%), large pore size (36.5 µm), and excellent swelling capacity (4144%). These beads were further tested for protein adsorption using bovine serum albumin (BSA) as a model, showing superior sorption capacity for ZnCl 2 –ethanol beads (107.9 mg g −1 at pH 3.0). Overall, the results demonstrate that processing conditions play a key role in controlling the structure–property relationships of lignocellulosic sisal fiber-derived beads and govern their performance in protein sorption, highlighting the versatility of this approach for designing high-performance, sustainable biomaterials.

title: International Migration from Nigeria: Determinants and Implications for Economic Development
source: IIARD INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ECONOMICS AND BUSINESS MANAGEMENT
summary: International migration is the movement of people across international borders for the purpose of settlement. Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation has witnessed significant international migration in recent decades driven by various facto
content: International migration is the movement of people across international borders for the purpose of settlement. Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation has witnessed significant international migration in recent decades driven by various factors, such as economic opportunity, social and political factors, environmental and climate factors but to mention a view. The objective of the study is to examine the leading causes, consequences and implications of Nigerians migrating abroad. Mixed-methods approach was employed for the study which include secondary data analysis, in-person and online interviews and survey research. A structured questionnaire was the instrument used for data collection. Through the purposive sampling technique, the opinion of fifty (50) respondents were obtained on the causes and effects of international migration out of Nigeria. The Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) was utilized for the data analysis. From the research it was revealed among others that the push and pull factors are the principal causes of international migration out of Nigeria. Part of recommendations given was that government should manage international migration for development and also make labour migration an explicit part of their development strategy.

title: Predicting Marching Band Ratings in Nebraska: A Quantitative Analysis of Socioeconomic Status and Geographic Variables
summary: Although the high school marching band has been a tradition in the United States for nearly a century, it is becoming increasingly rare in many rural areas. Despite economic barriers, some rural schools have overcome the challenges of their
content: Although the high school marching band has been a tradition in the United States for nearly a century, it is becoming increasingly rare in many rural areas. Despite economic barriers, some rural schools have overcome the challenges of their location and built successful instrumental music programs. Research on rural music education is vital because most new music educators in Nebraska will begin their careers teaching in rural schools. A quantitative study examined marching band performance in Nebraska, a highly rural state. The study reviewed NSBA State Marching Contest overall ratings from 2015 to 2024, along with a socioeconomic profile of the schools and communities the bands represent, utilizing a multiple linear regression model. Results indicated a statistically insignificant linear combination prediction at the conventional α = .05 level, F(3, 56) = 2.637, p = .058 (R2 = .124), but a statistically significant association between FRPL eligibility and weaker overall ratings. These findings can guide preservice and current teachers in shaping their teaching philosophies and pedagogical practices, helping them design successful programs grounded in research-based practices despite socioeconomic challenges. These implications have a meaningful impact on music education, and the results could also benefit other school music programs, such as band, choir, orchestra, and elementary music. Likewise, these findings could support rural school music programs across the United States, informing recommended future research that could shape local, state, and federal policy, leading to more equal access and funding for music education.

title: Expert perceptions on women’s involvement in illegal wildlife trade networks
summary: Illegal wildlife trade is often male dominated at harvest, yet women's roles across supply chains are under-examined. This study adds substantially to this growing body of knowledge drawing on 112 semi-structured interviews with law enforce
content: Illegal wildlife trade is often male dominated at harvest, yet women's roles across supply chains are under-examined. This study adds substantially to this growing body of knowledge drawing on 112 semi-structured interviews with law enforcement and illegal wildlife trade experts in South Africa, Hong Kong, and Canada. We show women participate in finance and money laundering, brokerage, logistics, retail, online marketing, and couriering, with occasional leadership. Women are also strategically used to shield men. Drawing on conservation and feminist criminology-specifically women's liberation and strain/marginalization perspectives-alongside an intersectional framework, we interpret role differentiation across contexts. While perceptions-based data and male-dominated enforcement may bias visibility, patterns are consistent. We recommend gender-competent, intersectional counter-illegal wildlife trade strategies and better gender-disaggregated data.

title: Integrity-based or profit-oriented: Confucian culture and corporate green fraud behaviour
summary: Aim: This study aimed to explore how Confucian culture, as a form of informal institution, influences the incidence of corporate green fraud in China. In the broader context of China’s transition toward a green economy, the research sheds l
content: Aim: This study aimed to explore how Confucian culture, as a form of informal institution, influences the incidence of corporate green fraud in China. In the broader context of China’s transition toward a green economy, the research sheds light on the governance function of traditional cultural values in promoting environmentally responsible corporate behaviour. Methodology: Using a panel dataset of A-share listed firms in China from 2008 to 2020, the study employs empirical analysis to examine the relationship between the prevalence of Confucian culture and corporate green fraud. It further conducts mechanism and heterogeneity analyses to identify potential transmission channels and contextual factors influencing this relationship. Results: The results reveal that Confucian culture significantly reduces the occurrence of corporate green fraud. This relationship is mediated by enhanced green innovation capabilities, greater financial transparency, and improved quality of environmental disclosures. The impact of Confucian culture also varies across companies based on their geographic location, level of external scrutiny, and operational performance. Additionally, the presence of alternative cultural influences moderates the effectiveness of Confucian norms in curbing green fraud. Implications and recommendations: The research findings suggest that informal institutions can mitigate corporate green fraud. Future studies should investigate the potential influence of other informal institutional factors on corporate green fraud. Originality/value: This paper contributes to the literature by providing novel empirical evidence on the role of traditional culture in environmental governance. It highlights the value of leveraging cultural heritage in the fight against greenwashing and offers policy insights for promoting corporate environmental integrity during China’s green economic transformation.

title: From FoMO to clicks: Understanding young people's behavior toward retargeted advertisements
summary: The rapid advancements in artificial intelligence have led to highly personalized and programmatic advertising, using retargeted advertisements that incorporate Fear of Missing Out (FoMO) appeals to enhance customer engagement. Retargeted a
content: The rapid advancements in artificial intelligence have led to highly personalized and programmatic advertising, using retargeted advertisements that incorporate Fear of Missing Out (FoMO) appeals to enhance customer engagement. Retargeted advertisements chase customers after they leave a website without conversion. This study uniquely investigates the persistent influence of retargeted advertisements on young people in the digital sphere, particularly when synergistically combined with FoMO appeals. It further applies the Theory of Planned Behavior to understand its impact. FoMO is conceptualized in this study as a higher-order construct, comprising four lower-order constructs: scarcity, urgency, social proof, and loss aversion. These were included in a self-administered survey with a sample of 480 respondents. Data were analyzed using PLS-SEM. Findings reveal a strong relationship between FoMO and attitude, subjective norms, and the intention to click on retargeted advertisements. Attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control significantly influence young people's intention to click, ultimately influencing behavior. The influence of FoMO appeals on subjective norms and behavioral intentions is more pronounced among men. Conversely, attitude serves as the primary precursor of intention to click for women. These findings offer crucial theoretical and practical implications for stakeholders navigating the evolving digital advertising landscape.

title: Bridging Nepal’s SDG Deficit: Progress Assessment, Bottlenecks, and Strategic Pathways to Agenda 2030
summary: This study is review based structural approach to review Nepal's progress in the SDG implementation of Agenda 2030. The study was focused on evaluate baseline and midterm progress with respect to ultimate target 2030 at the sub-national lev
content: This study is review based structural approach to review Nepal's progress in the SDG implementation of Agenda 2030. The study was focused on evaluate baseline and midterm progress with respect to ultimate target 2030 at the sub-national level. The study used descriptive approach that incorporates quantitative information from national reviews on fiscal and administrative contexts. The results indicate a clear dichotomy in the development path of Nepal. Nepal has made significant improvements in the simple indicators of physical access and ecological conservation such as access to electricity, drinking water and forest cover but is making poor progress in the more complex indicators of economic and institutional development such as industrial value added to GDP and youth employment. This study highlights the systemic challenges that limit progress such as capital expenditure that takes place in the last month of the fiscal year (known as “AsareBikas” or “Asar development”), the lack of technical staff on the ground, weak inter-governmental coordination, and continued use of national average statistics that mask local poverty cycles. The public sustainable development financing gap is huge, about NPR 426 billion in Nepal, which is approximately 13.4 percent of the annual national investment need of NPR 3.023 trillion. In order to deal with this implementation gap by 2030, the study suggests a four-pillar strategic roadmap: Updating the Public Procurement Act and enacting Civil Service Act, creating a shared regional technical human resource pool, digitizing sub-national data system and mobilizing innovative green financing instruments. The findings provide policy guidance that can be used to drive measurable, equitable outcomes to realize Nepal's SDG commitments while upholding the principle of Leave no one Behind(LNOB).

title: Early Near-Infrared Excess and Rapid Disk-Corona Evolution in the Tidal Disruption Event 2024aepd
summary: Abstract We present multi-wavelength observations of the tidal disruption event (TDE) 2024aepd, spanning primarily the first ∼300 days after discovery. A prominent near-infrared (NIR) excess is detected as early as ∼40 days. Its nearly flat
content: Abstract We present multi-wavelength observations of the tidal disruption event (TDE) 2024aepd, spanning primarily the first ∼300 days after discovery. A prominent near-infrared (NIR) excess is detected as early as ∼40 days. Its nearly flat power-law spectrum strongly deviates from the Rayleigh-Jeans tail of the UV-optical blackbody. Although a conventional dust-echo origin cannot be completely ruled out, free–free emission from a reprocessing photospheric envelope provides a more plausible explanation. The spectral break between the UV-optical and NIR components shifts to higher frequencies, while the inferred density-profile index remains nearly constant, suggesting evolving reprocessing conditions within a broadly unchanged density structure. In addition, the X-ray spectrum is initially dominated by a thermal disk component accompanied by a hard excess. From ∼178 days onward, the spectrum becomes power-law dominated and subsequently hardens, indicating the rapid emergence and strengthening of a hot corona. These results provide evidence for frequency-dependent reprocessing at early times and for the rapid development of a disk-corona system, placing new constraints on the structure and evolution of the reprocessing layer around supermassive black holes.

title: The UK Model of Economic Regulation After 40 Years: Time for a Reset?
summary: Abstract In 1984 the UK embarked on a new approach to economic regulation, which influenced the design of regulation in many countries. While it has largely stood the test of time, the UK model of economic regulation is perceived by some to
content: Abstract In 1984 the UK embarked on a new approach to economic regulation, which influenced the design of regulation in many countries. While it has largely stood the test of time, the UK model of economic regulation is perceived by some to be costly, complex, and divorced from some of its original aims. This paper describes the UK model, identifies common trends in its evolution, and critically evaluates possible adaptations to address the problems identified. Given the significant influence of the UK model internationally, the analysis offers insights for other jurisdictions on issues such as regulatory independence, institutional design, and how to deal with multiple policy agendas, accountability, appeals, and governance structures. It also highlights how the institutional context affects the outcomes of key industrial organization ideas -- such as privatization, incentive regulation, and structural separation.

title: Digital inclusive finance and eco-development efficiency in China’s pastoral regions: conditional, nonlinear and heterogeneous evidence from Inner Mongolia
summary: Introduction Ecologically fragile pastoral regions face the dual challenge of improving livelihoods while maintaining ecosystem stability, making them critical areas for achieving sustainable and resilient food systems. Methods This study e
content: Introduction Ecologically fragile pastoral regions face the dual challenge of improving livelihoods while maintaining ecosystem stability, making them critical areas for achieving sustainable and resilient food systems. Methods This study examines the association between digital inclusive finance (DIF) and eco-development efficiency (EDE) using 2016–2023 panel data from 54 pastoral and semi-pastoral counties in Inner Mongolia, China. EDE was measured using an input-oriented BCC-DEA model, and the association between DIF and EDE was examined using panel Tobit regressions. Results The results show that the ecological role of DIF in pastoral regions is conditional rather than inherently positive or negative, varying with structural conditions, county types, development stages, and broader contextual factors. After controlling for common time trends, DIF is significantly negatively associated with EDE, and correlated random effects analysis indicates that this pattern largely reflects persistent cross-county structural differences rather than short-term within-county changes. Among the DIF dimensions, coverage breadth is significantly negatively associated with EDE, whereas usage depth and digitalization level show no significant associations with EDE after controlling for common time trends. Industrial structure further moderates this negative association, suggesting that local structural conditions may shape the ecological role of DIF. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the negative association between DIF and EDE is mainly observed in pure pastoral counties, whereas no significant association is found in semi-pastoral counties. Nonlinear analysis reveals an inverted U-shaped relationship, indicating that the ecological implications of DIF vary across development stages. Discussion These findings suggest that digital inclusive finance policies in pastoral regions should shift from scale-oriented expansion toward quality-oriented, structurally compatible, and ecologically guided development, thereby better supporting green development and sustainable pastoral food systems.

title: APEW-Fed: adaptive privacy-aware ensemble weighting for federated anomaly detection in enterprise resource planning systems
summary: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems are high-value targets for fraud owing to the sensitive financial and operational data they process. Anomaly detection in such systems faces a fundamental tension: centralising data for accurate de
content: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems are high-value targets for fraud owing to the sensitive financial and operational data they process. Anomaly detection in such systems faces a fundamental tension: centralising data for accurate detection conflicts with privacy regulations such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the United States' Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX). We present APEW-Fed, a federated ensemble framework that resolves this tension through three provably complementary mechanisms. First, Adaptive Privacy-Aware Ensemble Weighting (APEW) frames model fusion as a privacy-penalised optimisation problem and derives closed-form dynamic weights that up-weight privacy-efficient, high-confidence detectors. Second, Feature-Sensitivity Calibrated Differential Privacy (FS-CDP) partitions features into sensitivity tiers and allocates per-tier Gaussian noise budgets that provably minimise total noise variance subject to a global Rényi DP constraint. Third, Federated Anomaly Score Calibration (FASC) reconciles heterogeneous score distributions across clients via differentially private quantile sketches under secure aggregation. Integrating Isolation Forest, a federated autoencoder trained with per-step DP-SGD, adaptive DBSCAN, and gradient boosting, we evaluate on 243,531 real-world ERP transactions with 5000 expert-annotated anomalies and validate on two public benchmarks: the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection dataset and the NSL-KDD network intrusion dataset. APEW-Fed achieves 93.5% F1-score at [Formula: see text] RDP-only 2.7 percentage points below the non-private centralised baseline-while reducing communication cost by 94% versus FedAvg. On a strictly unbiased uniform-only evaluation subset (2500 transactions, no score-based enrichment), APEW-Fed achieves 92.1% F1, confirming that the headline result is not an artefact of the annotation sampling design. Membership inference attack success is 51.2%, near-random guessing, confirming strong empirical privacy.

title: Forbear That Wicked Cant: Malthusian ‘Zero Sum’ Theory, Eugenics, and World Population Control
summary: This dissertation traces the history of an idea: the “zero-sum” theory of human nature and humanity’s relationship with the natural world that lies at the core of the Malthusian worldview. Grounded in the belief that life is a ruthless stru
content: This dissertation traces the history of an idea: the “zero-sum” theory of human nature and humanity’s relationship with the natural world that lies at the core of the Malthusian worldview. Grounded in the belief that life is a ruthless struggle over scarce resources and that human beings are destined to reproduce beyond the earth’s “carrying capacity,” Malthusianism provided the key intellectual foundations for Darwin’s theory of evolution, which later informed the rise of eugenics. Although eugenics lost much of its scientific legitimacy and moral authority after the Holocaust and the Nuremberg Trials, many American eugenicists and eugenics organizations remained committed to their program of genetic improvement and to the Malthusian assumptions that underpinned them. During the Cold War, an explicitly “zero-sum” framework for understanding population growth and economic development became institutionalized within the U.S. government, the United Nations, and major international family planning organizations. Driven by fears of communism, resource scarcity, and ecological collapse, U.S. policymakers led a global effort to curb fertility rates, particularly in the developing world. Although many of these catastrophic predictions never materialized, Malthusian assumptions continue to exert significant influence in the twenty-first century, including within the United Nations and affiliated NGOs.

title: Impact of oil price shocks on Japanese industries
summary: Oil price shocks characterized by sharp increases in crude oil prices have historically had severe adverse effects on the Japanese economy. However, how such disruptions manifest themselves at the industry level and what adjustments they in
content: Oil price shocks characterized by sharp increases in crude oil prices have historically had severe adverse effects on the Japanese economy. However, how such disruptions manifest themselves at the industry level and what adjustments they induce remain insufficiently understood. This study defines the Net Oil Price Increase (NOPI)—constructed following Hamilton (1996, 2003)—as an oil price shock and examines its effects on production and prices in the Aggregate Industry and 18 Japanese manufacturing industries. By comparing the aggregate and industry-level responses, this study seeks to provide a multifaceted interpretation of how oil price shocks affect Japanese industries. The analysis uses two subsamples: January 1978 to December 2002 and January 2003 to December 2019. The results indicate that the Aggregate Industry is affected by supply-side constraints in both periods, although the timing of these effects differs between the two subsamples. By contrast, the responses of individual industries vary substantially across periods. In the pre-2003 subsample, many individual industries exhibit supply-side effects similar to those observed for the Aggregate Industry. However, in the post-2003 subsample demand-side responses associated with precautionary stockpiling, the postponement of purchases, and price negotiations are observed. These results show that the effects of oil price shocks are not confined to supply-side channels within individual industries, but vary across industries, with both their magnitude and transmission channels changing substantially across sample periods.

title: Pricing Analytics
summary: This updated and expanded second edition has the same theme as the first: the price, the number, someone puts on a product to help consumers decide to buy that product, comes from statistically modeling data. Five new chapters provide a wid
content: This updated and expanded second edition has the same theme as the first: the price, the number, someone puts on a product to help consumers decide to buy that product, comes from statistically modeling data. Five new chapters provide a wider perspective on pricing analytics to more effectively develop elasticities and pricing strategies. This book gives readers the statistical modeling tools needed to get the number to put on a product, based on economic and statistical principles and theory. It covers elasticities, methodologies for analyzing customer choices including conjoint analysis, pricing segmentation, big data and econometric models—now with improved explanations and developments. The second edition adds discussion of three important and advanced topics: simulations for testing strategies under different conditions such as scenario analysis, AI applications for elasticity estimation and dynamic pricing, and the impacts of tariffs. A comprehensive and essential resource for analysts—economists, statisticians, or market researchers—who must estimate the optimal price for a product or service, this book is also a helpful guide for upper-level students in analytics disciplines.

title: Coerced labour patterns in the Cape Colony, c. 1806–1826
summary: Abstract Multiple forms of coerced labour co‐existed in the early 19th‐century Cape Colony. This study examines changes in coerced labour force composition. Using annual taxation and census records, we examine district‐ and household‐level
content: Abstract Multiple forms of coerced labour co‐existed in the early 19th‐century Cape Colony. This study examines changes in coerced labour force composition. Using annual taxation and census records, we examine district‐ and household‐level changes in reported enslaved, Recaptured African and indigenous Khoesan labour. In a novel contribution, we show the increasing importance of Khoe labour in the Cape District both as an increasing proportion of the coerced labour force and in the number of households reporting Khoesan labourers. We find no equivalent shift to Khoe labour in Stellenbosch District. This contributes to understanding the role of indigenous labour in colonial contexts.

title: Green Public Financial Management and Sustainable Development
summary: The systematic review brings together the research on PFM and sustainable development, concentrating on the form of governance and climate policy and fiscal innovation. The article is based on 50 studies that cover Asia, Europe, Latin Ameri
content: The systematic review brings together the research on PFM and sustainable development, concentrating on the form of governance and climate policy and fiscal innovation. The article is based on 50 studies that cover Asia, Europe, Latin America, and Africa to provide an analysis of three typologies of governance, climate budgeting, and emergent financial instruments that are used to promote environmental sustainability. The results show that a multi-level governance and financial decentralization are beneficial to local climate action, but they are usually limited by the coordination challenges and the capacity of the locality. Ecological fiscal transfers, climate budget tagging, and green bonds are some of the instruments that enhance transparency and mobilization of climate finance but their participation is spotty across countries. In general, efficient green PFM needs to be more institutionalized, the frameworks of evaluation should be streamlined, and principled fiscal innovation should be scalable to bring the public finance systems to the point of sustainability.

title: From Digital Transformation to Sustained Competitive Advantage: How Strategic Orientation, Technology Sophistication, and Adaptive Capability Drive Operational Efficiency
summary: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in emerging markets face a critical challenge: how to leverage digital transformation to improve efficiency and sustain competitive advantage despite constrained financial and human resources. This
content: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in emerging markets face a critical challenge: how to leverage digital transformation to improve efficiency and sustain competitive advantage despite constrained financial and human resources. This study addresses this problem by examining how distinct dimensions of digital transformation affect SME operational efficiency and, in turn, sustained competitive advantage. Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV) and Industrial Organization-Based Strategy (IO), the present study conceptualizes digital transformation through three theoretically distinct sub-dimensions, digital strategic orientation (DSO), digital adaptive capability (DAC), and digital technology sophistication (DTS), and model operational efficiency as a mediating pathway to sustained competitive advantage. Data collected via a structured survey administered to 216 Turkish manufacturing and service SMEs operating in Istanbul were analyzed using variance-based structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The findings reveal that all three digital transformation sub-dimensions positively and significantly influence operational efficiency, which in turn strongly predicts sustained competitive advantage. A formal mediation analysis confirms that operational efficiency mediates the effects of all three digital transformation dimensions on sustained competitive advantage, with partial mediation for digital strategic orientation and indirect-only mediation for digital adaptive capability and digital technology sophistication. These results advance theoretical understanding by demonstrating that digital transformation operates as a capability-building process consistent with RBV logic, and that strategic digital orientation, rather than technological sophistication, is the dominant driver of efficiency gains. Practically, the findings indicate that SMEs should prioritize embedding digital strategy into corporate planning, developing structured digital upskilling programs for managers and employees, and investing in scalable cloud-based and AI-enabled infrastructure to achieve cost efficiency and competitive positioning.

title: Green transition: digital inclusion and renewable energy in Africa’s sustainability journey
source: International Journal of Energy Sector Management
summary: Purpose This study aims to investigate the relationship between digital financial inclusion, renewable energy consumption and environmental sustainability in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). It aims to examine how digital financial systems facilit
content: Purpose This study aims to investigate the relationship between digital financial inclusion, renewable energy consumption and environmental sustainability in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). It aims to examine how digital financial systems facilitate access to clean energy and enhance environmental outcomes. Specifically, the study evaluates the direct and indirect (mediating) role of renewable energy consumption in linking digital financial inclusion to environmental sustainability, addressing challenges of energy poverty, financial exclusion and environmental degradation in the region. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a quantitative research design using cross-sectional data from 44 SSA countries for the year 2023. It is grounded in endogenous growth theory, which frames digital financial inclusion as a technology-driven enabler of sustainable development. The analysis uses Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) to examine both direct and mediating relationships among digital financial inclusion, renewable energy consumption and environmental sustainability. Findings The results reveal that digital financial inclusion is positively associated with renewable energy consumption and with improved environmental sustainability in SSA. Renewable energy consumption also has a strong positive effect on environmental sustainability. Further, it plays a significant mediating role in the relationship between digital financial inclusion and environmental sustainability. This indicates that digital finance enhances environmental outcomes both directly and indirectly by facilitating investment and access to clean energy technologies. Research limitations/implications These findings carry critical implications for policy: governments and regulators in SSA should embed digital financial inclusion strategies within national renewable energy and climate action frameworks, leveraging mobile money ecosystems, fintech-enabled pay-as-you-go models and digital microcredit platforms as integrated instruments for simultaneously advancing clean energy access and improving environmental sustainability, in direct support of Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 7 (affordable and clean energy), SDG 13 (climate action) and SDG 1 (no poverty). Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by integrating digital financial inclusion into the energy–environment nexus within SSA.
